blocks.text: A 62-year-old man with myeloma develops an enlarged tongue, ankle swelling, heavy proteinuria and a stiff, thickened heart on echocardiography. A kidney biopsy stained with Congo red looks pink-red, then turns apple-green when viewed between crossed polarising filters. The organs of this patient are being replaced by a protein that should never have formed a solid.

blocks.markdown: **Amyloidosis** is a group of disorders in which abnormally folded proteins aggregate as insoluble fibrils that deposit in the extracellular space and damage tissue. Amyloid appears as pink, amorphous, hyaline material on haematoxylin and eosin staining. All amyloid, regardless of its protein precursor, has the same underlying structure: a **cross-beta-pleated sheet** fibrillar arrangement, plus a minor component of P component (serum amyloid P) and glycosaminoglycans.

blocks.title: Amyloid
blocks.text: Amyloid is an extracellular deposit of insoluble protein fibrils with a cross-beta-pleated sheet conformation, giving characteristic staining properties (Congo red) and resistance to proteolysis, irrespective of the precursor protein.

blocks.markdown:
### How misfolding leads to deposition

Proteins fold into a defined three-dimensional shape guided by chaperones. Some proteins can adopt an alternative misfolded conformation rich in beta-sheet. Misfolded molecules can nucleate and self-assemble into oligomers and then stable fibrils that are resistant to degradation by proteases. Misfolding is promoted by (1) a **mutation** that destabilises the protein (hereditary amyloid, for example transthyretin variants), (2) **sustained high concentrations** of a normally soluble protein (for example overproduction of light chains or serum amyloid A), or (3) **abnormal proteolytic processing** of a precursor to a fragment that aggregates (for example amyloid beta from amyloid precursor protein in Alzheimer disease). The fibrils deposit in tissues and, because they cannot be cleared, they expand and compress parenchymal cells, causing pressure atrophy and organ failure.

rows: Immunoglobulin light chains from plasma cell clone
Plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma or monoclonal gammopathy
Heart, kidney, tongue, nerves, gut, liver
Serum amyloid A (acute phase protein from the liver)
Chronic inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic infection such as tuberculosis, familial Mediterranean fever)
Senile systemic amyloidosis; hereditary familial amyloid polyneuropathy
blocks.caption: Major amyloid types and associated disease.

blocks.title: Choosing AL or AA
blocks.prompt: (a) A 70-year-old woman with a plasma cell neoplasm has nephrotic syndrome and macroglossia. (b) A 45-year-old man with 20 years of rheumatoid arthritis develops proteinuria and hepatosplenomegaly. Name the amyloid type and precursor for each.

steps.text: (a) A clonal plasma cell proliferation produces monoclonal light chains, which misfold and deposit: AL amyloidosis. Macroglossia and cardiac involvement are typical of AL.

(b) Chronic inflammation raises IL-6 and the liver produces large amounts of serum amyloid A, an acute phase protein, which is cleaved and deposits: AA amyloidosis, with renal, hepatic and splenic involvement.
The key discriminator is the setting: plasma cell disorder (AL) versus chronic inflammatory disease (AA).

blocks.answer: (a) AL, precursor immunoglobulin light chain; (b) AA, precursor serum amyloid A.

blocks.markdown:
### Congo red staining and polarised light

The standard diagnostic stain is **Congo red**. Under ordinary light amyloid stains **pink to red**. When the section is examined under **polarised light**, amyloid shows **apple-green birefringence**. The birefringence arises because Congo red dye molecules align along the parallel beta-pleated sheets, and is a property of the cross-beta fibril structure, not of the particular precursor protein. Other stains: thioflavin T gives fluorescence. Tissue diagnosis is usually by biopsy of an affected organ, abdominal fat pad or rectal biopsy; the amyloid type is then confirmed by immunohistochemistry or mass spectrometry because management depends on the type.

blocks.title: Interpreting the stain
blocks.prompt: A renal biopsy has glomerular deposits that are pink on H&E, stain orange-red with Congo red under normal light, and show apple-green colour under crossed polarisers. What does this show and why is type determination still necessary?

steps.text: Congo red positivity with apple-green birefringence under polarised light identifies amyloid, regardless of the precursor.
The common cross-beta-sheet structure explains why all amyloids give the same pattern.
The treatment and prognosis differ between AL (treat the plasma cell clone) and AA (treat the underlying inflammation), so immunohistochemistry or mass spectrometry is needed to type the deposit.

blocks.answer: Amyloid is present; the type must be determined separately.

blocks.markdown:
### Organ consequences

**Kidney** is most commonly affected in systemic amyloidosis, producing proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome and renal failure. **Heart** (restrictive cardiomyopathy with stiff, thickened walls, arrhythmias and conduction disease) is particularly common in AL and ATTR. **Liver and spleen** show enlargement with a waxy cut surface. **Nerves** may be involved (neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome), and the gut (malabsorption). Amyloid is weakly eosinophilic and deposits are ischaemic by compression of vessels in the walls.

items: Amyloid deposits are extracellular and show Congo red apple-green birefringence.
AL is associated with plasma cell disorders; AA with chronic inflammation.
Localised amyloid (for example in the brain in Alzheimer disease) is distinct from systemic disease.
Treatment targets the source of the precursor protein (teaching context).

blocks.title: Link stain to structure
blocks.text: Apple-green birefringence is a property of the beta-pleated sheet structure, not of the precursor. That is why Congo red identifies all amyloid types, and why a separate test is needed to tell AL from AA.

points: Amyloid is formed when misfolded proteins aggregate into insoluble cross-beta-sheet fibrils that deposit in tissue and resist degradation.
AL amyloid derives from immunoglobulin light chains in plasma cell disorders; AA amyloid derives from serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation.
Congo red stains amyloid pink-red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light, independent of the precursor protein.

questions.stem: What is the characteristic appearance of amyloid stained with Congo red and viewed under polarised light?

distractorRationale.d: That describes monosodium urate crystals in gout.

questions.explanation: Congo red-stained amyloid shows apple-green birefringence under crossed polarising filters, due to alignment of dye along beta-pleated sheets.

questions.stem: Which precursor protein forms amyloid in a patient with multiple myeloma?
questions.explanation: A clonal plasma cell population produces excess monoclonal light chains that misfold into AL amyloid. Serum amyloid A is the precursor in reactive disease.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with long-standing Crohn disease develops proteinuria. A renal biopsy shows Congo red-positive deposits. Which precursor is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: AA amyloid in chronic inflammatory disease.
distractorRationale.b: AL needs a plasma cell disorder.

questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation sustains IL-6-driven production of serum amyloid A by the liver, which forms AA amyloid in the kidney and other organs.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how protein misfolding leads to amyloid deposition?

options.text: Misfolded proteins adopt beta-sheet conformations that self-assemble into insoluble fibrils resistant to degradation
Normally folded proteins are secreted into cells and cross-linked by collagen

questions.correctOptionText: Misfolded proteins adopt beta-sheet conformations that self-assemble into insoluble fibrils resistant to degradation
questions.explanation: A misfolded beta-sheet-rich form nucleates fibril growth, and the resulting fibrils resist proteases so they accumulate extracellularly.

questions.stem: True or false: The Congo red apple-green birefringence is specific to AL amyloid and absent in AA amyloid.
questions.explanation: Birefringence arises from the shared cross-beta-sheet structure, so all amyloid types show it. Typing requires additional techniques.

questions.stem: A man receiving haemodialysis for 15 years develops carpal tunnel syndrome and joint pain, and a biopsy shows amyloid. Which pathogenic mechanism fits best?

options.text: Sustained high levels of a normally soluble protein that cannot be cleared, promoting aggregation

questions.correctOptionText: Sustained high levels of a normally soluble protein that cannot be cleared, promoting aggregation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: beta-2 microglobulin accumulates because dialysis does not clear it well.
distractorRationale.c: No plasma cell disorder is described.

questions.explanation: Beta-2 microglobulin is poorly removed by dialysis and accumulates, aggregating into amyloid in joints and tendons. High concentration is one route to misfolding and deposition.

questions.stem: A patient with AL amyloidosis has a serum free light chain level of 450 mg/L, and the laboratory upper reference limit (varies by laboratory) is 30 mg/L. Calculate by what factor the level exceeds the upper reference limit.
questions.explanation: 450/30 = 15, so the level is 15 times the upper limit. Sustained high concentrations of a precursor protein promote misfolding and fibril formation in AL amyloidosis.

questions.stem: A renal biopsy contains 40 glomeruli, of which 28 show Congo red-positive amyloid deposits. Calculate the percentage of glomeruli involved.
questions.explanation: 28/40 = 0.70, so 70% of the sampled glomeruli are involved. Extensive glomerular deposition accounts for the heavy proteinuria and renal impairment of amyloidosis.

Common cross-beta-sheet structure for all amyloid types

questions.stem: Distinguish AL from AA amyloidosis in terms of precursor protein, associated disease and organs affected, and explain how you would confirm amyloid on biopsy.
markingGuide: AL: immunoglobulin light chains, plasma cell clone (myeloma/monoclonal gammopathy), heart, kidney, tongue, nerves
AA: serum amyloid A acute phase protein, chronic inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic infection), kidney, liver, spleen
Congo red stain: pink-red in normal light
Typing by immunohistochemistry or mass spectrometry because treatment differs
questions.explanation: The setting of chronic inflammation versus plasma cell disease separates AA from AL. Congo red confirms amyloid but does not identify the type.
